prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which many neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength enable frequency measurement at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange my preferred configuration is unchanged: the optical lattice clock alone, credited to Katori and Ye. The scientific core has not been challenged by anyone. The magic-wavelength condition cancels the trapping light shift, so many neutral atoms can be interrogated at once without the motional and Stark-shift limits that constrain single-ion clocks. Fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 have been reproduced and compared in many independent laboratories, and the results already feed the preparation for redefining the second, relativistic geodesy, and bounds on varying constants and dark-sector couplings. The first round also sharpened my view on credit: Katori proposed the concept and realised the first strontium lattice clock, and Ye drove accuracy, stability and the many-body regime, so the two names map onto two distinct and necessary contributions. I have tightened the citation to name the magic-wavelength many-atom lattice explicitly, so that it describes the invention itself and not optical clocks or precision spectroscopy in general. Broad support is not my argument. I hold the position because the concept, the demonstration, the replication and the consequences each survive scrutiny separately, and because no other shortlisted entry combines a comparably complete maturity record with a credit set that does not force an arbitrary cut.
statement.case_against: The overlap with earlier recognition remains the honest reservation. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb and laser precision spectroscopy, the 2012 prize covered control of single quantum systems including ion-based clocks, and the lattice clock depends on both. I judge the lattice clock a different concept, but a committee member who sees optical timekeeping as already well served is not being unreasonable. Credit at the edges is also not fully captured by two names: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Bloom, and the Paris and PTB groups made real contributions, and the weighting of Katori's early proposal and demonstration against parallel work rests partly on my recollection, not on verified records. Finally, the redefinition of the second has not yet been adopted, so part of the downstream payoff is prospective. I do not think waiting would improve the scientific case, but it is a legitimate timing argument.

responses.point: Argues that the lattice clock is a refinement of a precision-spectroscopy tradition honoured twice, and that topological insulators opened a new classification of phases and so carry greater conceptual novelty, while naming B048 only as an alternative.
responses.response: I take the novelty argument seriously, but I think it compares unlike things. A new classification of phases is conceptual novelty of one kind; a new route to a measurement regime that was previously closed is novelty of another, and the magic-wavelength lattice is a genuinely new concept, not a refinement of the comb or of ion control. My larger difficulty with B019 is still credit. The HgTe proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is what made the Molenkamp experiment possible, and a Kane, Mele and Molenkamp trio leaves it outside, while the 2016 topology prize narrows the headroom. A Z2-focused citation would help but would not resolve that omission. B019 therefore stays as my alternative, and I would move toward it only if the committee settled the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang question in a way I find defensible.

responses.point: Holds B028 first, argues that broad agreement on a clean attribution does not make B048 more significant than a mature instrument invention, and reads my own note on the pending redefinition of the second as a timing argument that does not justify ranking the clock higher.
responses.response: I accept your correction that broad agreement and clean attribution are not measures of significance, and I have tried not to rest on them. Both the clock and aberration correction are inventions that changed what can be measured. I still rank the clock higher for two reasons. First, its result is a physical regime, 1e-18 fractional uncertainty, that opened new science in constants, geodesy and dark-sector searches, and not only a better instrument for existing studies. Second, the credit problem you flag, Krivanek and STEM correction left outside a TEM-only trio, is more acute than the edge-credit question for the clock. On the timing point, I would say the redefinition is the consequence of the clock's demonstrated performance, not a precondition for the discovery. I appreciate that you would regard B048 as a defensible outcome, and I would regard B028 as a serious, well-argued case and not a poor one.

responses.point: Moves from circuit QED to B048 as the cleanest attribution on the list, keeps B003 as an alternative, and notes that choosing atomic precision measurement spreads recognition after the 2025 circuit prize.
responses.response: I agree with your reading of the attribution and I find your timing point about the 2025 circuit prize relevant, though I would not make field rotation a reason on its own, and I do not think you do. On B003 I keep my earlier qualification: the Cirac-Zoller theory is outstanding, but the 2012 prize already recognised Wineland for trapped-ion control, and Monroe and other ion groups have experimental claims that Blatt alone does not cover. I would not add B003 as a second part, because that would turn a clean two-name prize into a three-name configuration with a visible attribution dispute. I appreciate that you disclosed your closeness to circuit QED while moving, and I read your shift as reasoned.

responses.point: Expresses that the lattice clock survives scrutiny on every axis, but cautions that broad opening support may only reflect the consensus safe option among several experimentalists, and doubts whether Katori and Ye alone cover the field.
responses.response: Your caution about a safe consensus option is fair, and it is the reason I tested the case on content. The three checks that matter to me are that the concept is original, the demonstration is decisive and the replication is independent, and the lattice clock passes all three. On the experimental-bias worry, I would point out that the strongest objections to B048 in this round came from B048 supporters themselves, which is not what a merely comfortable choice looks like. On Katori and Ye alone, I agree it is a judgment on credit and not a settled partition. I would still draw the line at the invention and its development, with Katori for concept and first realisation and Ye for record accuracy and many-body regimes, and I would not widen the set to three, because the next candidate for a third name would involve an arbitrary choice among Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and others.

responses.point: Argues that the already demonstrated impact outweighs the timing argument for waiting for the redefinition of the second, and that the citation must be drawn carefully against the comb and ion-clock prizes.
responses.response: I agree that demonstrated impact outweighs the timing argument, and I have moved from treating the redefinition as an open uncertainty to treating it as a modest one. The clock results are in hand regardless of the date of the formal decision. On wording, I have adopted the explicit magic-wavelength, many-neutral-atom language so that the citation cannot be read as covering optical clocks generally, which keeps it clear of the 2005 and 2012 prizes and of the ion-clock tradition. As an atomic physicist you are better placed than I am to judge whether the clock community would accept that wording, and I would defer to your reading if you think it undercredits the systematic-evaluation work.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will judge the lattice clock sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-quantum-system prizes; I think it is, but this is a judgment and not a settled fact.

Whether two names fairly cover the field given Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Bloom and the Paris and PTB groups, and how much my recollection of the priority sequence between Katori's early proposal and parallel work should be trusted without verified records.
Whether waiting for the formal redefinition of the second would improve the citation or only delay a recognition whose scientific basis is already complete.
Whether a second part such as B003 would be a better distribution of credit; I currently judge it would create a visible attribution dispute for little gain.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged and updated in light of the chair's question. I spent time in John Hall's laboratory, and Hall is a 2005 laureate whose comb work underlies lattice clocks. I regard this as field proximity and a possible indirect link to the precision-spectroscopy community, not a connection to Katori or Ye, and I do not see it as requiring recusal. For B003 and the quantum-memory area (B002) I have professional proximity through rare-earth-ion quantum memories, Lund colleagues, WACQT and Deep Light Vision; none of these involve the people credited on my preferred configuration, but I would recuse myself from B003 or B002 if either became the lead or a part of the final configuration. I report these so the committee can judge them.
